1: This briefing is Book 08 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, D N S, DHCP and eye-pam.
It's about governing the name and address layer as one control plane, across the data center, every cloud and the branch edge.
That may sound like plumbing, but here's the idea that drives the whole book.
Every connection starts with a name.
So whoever governs the name layer governs the enterprise.
We'll go in four steps: why D N S is now the control plane, what has to change, who owns it, and how to migrate it and run it.
Along the way you'll hear about failures that don't look like D N S failures at all, which is exactly why they're so hard to find.
2: Almost every network connection begins with a D N S query.
That's been true for a long time.
What's changed is how much the answer now decides.
In a hybrid, multi-cloud estate, D N S does six jobs its designers never planned for.
For example, one storage name can answer privately inside its network and publicly everywhere else.
D N S also picks which SaaS front door a user reaches, blocks known-bad domains before a connection is made, and carries certificate checks, because revocation endpoints are D N S names.
nist's 2026 guide puts it plainly: D N S has become more than a service; it's a security control.
Yet many estates run it on as many as five platforms that share no state.
The answer is one authoritative D D I policy plane, a requirement, not a product.
Here's what goes wrong without one.
3: Run those platforms separately and you get split-brain D N S: the same name giving different answers depending on where the query starts.
The problem is unplanned drift between systems with no shared state.
A workload in AWS only gets an Azure private endpoint's private address through a forwarding rule.
If that rule is missing or stale, the name still resolves, just to the public address.
Microsoft attributes roughly seventy percent of private-endpoint access-denied cases to exactly that.
The same drift happens with SaaS paths, and with security blocks that only apply on the resolver that answers.
Either way, the failure is silent, and it shows up as something else.
Changes come faster than any manual process can track.
Only a control plane that holds the policy keeps everything in step.

5: For twenty years, Active Directory has been the hidden D N S service of the on-premises network.
A domain's name becomes a zone, and every domain-joined machine points at the domain controllers for everything.
Each domain controller registers the locator records clients use to find it, and secure dynamic updates keep them current.
Entra ID inherits none of that.
It hosts no zones and publishes no locator records.
Yet hybrid-joined devices still go looking for a domain controller.
The locator records stay where domain controllers can register them securely, either on A D D N S or a D D I platform that accepts secure updates, until the last domain controller goes.
Everything else moves zone by zone, once it's been inventoried.
But even a well-designed name layer only works if queries actually reach it.
6: Every control in the policy plane assumes the query reaches it.
Three ordinary things decide whether it does, and none of them tells you when it doesn't.
SD-WAN can redirect branch D N S to a designated resolver, but that target has to be a real agency resolver on the network, not an agent on the device itself.
Some forms can be blocked at the firewall except to approved resolvers.
D N S over HTTPS hides inside normal web traffic, so it has to be governed on the endpoint, through browser and Windows policy.
One rogue server handing out its own resolver can move a whole subnet at once.
A D authorization doesn't stop that; switch protections do.
Next, a dependency that surprises people: certificates.
7: A certificate can be valid, unrevoked and issued for the right name, and still fail.
That's because every check that makes it trustworthy starts with a D N S lookup.
An agency's revocation list name exists only in A D D N S.
A workload in AWS can't resolve it without a forwarding rule.
The revocation check fails, a ticket gets opened against the P K I team, and the real cause can take days to find.
It proves where an answer came from and that it wasn't changed, but it doesn't encrypt anything.
Always sign external zones and the dot-gov delegations.
Sign internal zones only where the system's authorization requires it.
Validation stays on agency resolvers, because the cloud resolvers don't fully cover it.

8: Azure private endpoints are the most common source of private-address split-brain.
When you create one, Azure writes its record into a private zone, and public D N S points into that name.
You only get the private answer if your query reaches a resolver linked to that zone.
Every origin, whether on-premises, another cloud or the branch, forwards the service's public zone to the Azure D N S Private Resolver.
And Azure Government uses different zone names, so commercial rules don't carry over.
The Private Resolver is a bridge, not an authority, so you reach it by forwarding, never by delegation, and deploy one per region.
Addresses need the same discipline, with the enterprise eye-pam as the authority and the clouds reconciled against it.
Put it together, and you get one governed path.

10: In an A D estate, D N S belonged to whoever ran the domain controllers, and nobody really chose that.
A single policy plane concentrates that authority, so its owners have to be named on purpose, with one decider per decision.
The sponsor and C I O decide the platform model and when A D D N S and Windows DHCP retire.
The see-so and I S S O set the requirements, like designated resolvers, DNSSEC and logging.
The authorizing official accepts residual risk, including every standing exception.
The D N S and D D I team runs the plane and decides what the edge points at.
Network engineering configures it, and cloud teams consume it.
Record changes come in three classes.
Routine changes in a delegated namespace are pre-approved.
Policy-driven records follow a change-controlled policy.
And high-impact changes, like zones, delegations and forwarding, go to the change board.
So how do we get there?
11: The migration runs in six phases, from inventory and coexistence through to decommissioning A D D N S and DHCP, then hardening and evidence.
Each phase ends with a rollback point and a resolution test from every origin, not a calendar date.
Every move, whether it's a zone, a forwarder, a DHCP scope or a wave of clients, runs the same loop.
Import with a dry run, never moving the core zone or locator records.
Then switch, and watch, while the old authority keeps answering.
One warning from Azure: removing a network link deletes the records registered through it, and they can't be restored.
And decommissioning is gated, never scheduled.
The old servers retire only after the records resolve cleanly for a sustained period, parallel operation passes, and failover is tested.
Then the plane has to run every day.
12: One policy plane is only an improvement if divisions can still run their own networks through it.
So each division gets a scope over its own zones, addresses and DHCP, with manager, operator and auditor roles.
Automation is held to the same scopes.
Infrastructure as code, ticketing workflows and certificate automation all go through one API and one audit trail.
Locator records are checked from every site, every fifteen minutes, until the last domain controller retires.
Drift reports compare the source of truth with every copy, and hygiene jobs catch stale and dangling records.
The evidence floor is the federal logging memo.
It doesn't name D N S, but its retention rules apply to it.
Query logs, including encrypted queries, and DHCP lease history are how the name layer meets it.
And lease history is what turns an address into a device.

14: First, authorize a single authoritative D D I policy plane and give it an owner, typically the enterprise architecture or network operations lead.
Second, have that owner settle the five configuration decisions within ninety days, and report the residual risk to the authorizing official.
Third, choose the platform on evidence: authorization at the right impact level, and quotes on the same assumptions.
And fourth, name the owners, one decider per decision.
The next step is Phase 1, the inventory.
Export every A D D N S zone, locator record, forwarder and DHCP scope, every edge redirect target and every revocation endpoint, before anyone touches a domain controller.

Govern the name layer as one plane, and it can carry the cloud, branch and identity transitions.
